extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patent claims under 35 U.S.C. §101 (Alice/Mayo framework), including when to use streamlined analysis, how to identify judicial exceptions, and how to formulate and support eligibility rejections. Focused on claim-by-claim analysis of abstract ideas, laws of nature, and natural phenomena and related procedural requirements for Office actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant Application / Insignificant Extra-Solution Activity
rubrics_metrics.description: For claim limitations that add insignificant extra-solution activity to the judicial exception (e.g., mere data gathering in conjunction with a law of nature or abstract idea), examiners should explain in an eligibility rejection why they do not meaningfully limit the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: cutting hair after first determining the hair style (In re Brown); printing or downloading generated menus (Ameranth). Some cases treat insignificant computer implementation as insignificant extra-solution activity (Fort Props.; Bancorp Servs.). Examiners should explain why such additions do not meaningfully limit the claim (for example, storing data as a final step to a process that only recites a mathematical relationship does not add a meaningful limitation). See MPEP §2106.05(f) and MPEP §2106.07(a) for more on formulating rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of Use and Technological Environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that merely indicate a field of use or technological environment in which to apply a judicial exception do not amount to significantly more than the exception itself and thus cannot integrate a judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic example: Parker v. Flook — limiting a formula to petrochemical use was token and insufficient. Contrast: Diamond v. Diehr where specific limitations acted in concert to transform a product. Affinity Labs shows limiting an abstract idea to cellular telephones did not supply an inventive concept. Courts often use 'technological environment' and 'field of use' interchangeably. Consider overlap with insignificant extra-solution activity (MPEP §2106.05(g)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of Insufficient Field-of-Use Limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Court-identified examples where limiting an abstract idea to a field of use or technological environment was insufficient to confer eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerated examples include: (i) administering 6-thioguanine to a specific patient population (Mayo); (ii) identifying participants as commodity providers/consumers (Bilski); (iii) limiting C = 2πr to wheel circumference (Flook); (iv) limiting audit-log monitoring to computer environment (FairWarning); (v) virus screening within telephone network/Internet (Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec); (vi) limiting collecting/analyzing/displaying results to electric power grid data (Electric Power Group v. Alstom); (vii) informing doctors to apply a law of nature to detect a polymorphism (Genetic Techs. v. Merial); (viii) budgeting implemented using 'communication medium' including Internet/phone (Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One); (ix) advertising-as-currency used on the Internet (Ultramercial); (x) requiring performance guarantees be performed online or using a computer/network (buySAFE v. Google). Examiners should consider these examples when assessing whether a limitation is merely a field-of-use restriction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined Analysis (Pathway A)
rubrics_metrics.description: For efficiency, examiners may use a streamlined eligibility analysis when the eligibility of the claim is self-evident (e.g., because the claim clearly improves a technology or computer functionality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The streamlined (Pathway A) analysis is appropriate only when eligibility is self-evident; results of streamlined analysis must be the same as the full analysis. If there is doubt whether the applicant is effectively seeking coverage for a judicial exception, the full Alice/Mayo analysis should be applied. A claim eligible under Step 2A (Pathway B) or Step 2B (Pathway C) would also be eligible under the streamlined analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility is Self-Evident — Examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of claims whose eligibility may be self-evident and thus suitable for streamlined analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a complex manufactured industrial product/process with meaningful limitations (e.g., a robotic arm assembly with control system using mathematical relationships); an artificial hip prosthesis coated with a naturally occurring mineral that does not attempt to tie up the mineral; products with ancillary nature-based components (e.g., cellphone with gold contact, plastic chair with wood trim). Such claims do not require full analysis to determine they are not attempting to tie up a judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear Improvement to Technology or Computer Functionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that clearly improve a technology or computer functionality may be not 'directed to' an abstract idea and thus can avoid the full eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit examples: Enfish (self-referential table for a database), McRO (automatic lip synchronization and facial expression animation) — these were found eligible at Step 1. If claims present a 'close call' (e.g., BASCOM filtering example), a full eligibility analysis should be performed. Only when claims clearly improve technology or computer functionality, or otherwise have self-evident eligibility, should the streamlined analysis be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulating and Supporting Rejections — General Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility rejections must be based on substantive law under 35 U.S.C. §101 as interpreted by judicial precedent; examiners must review the record as a whole and make claim-by-claim evaluations. The rejection must set forth a prima facie case of ineligibility that is clear and specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should review specification, claims, prosecution history, relevant case law, and any relevant prior art. Each claim should be considered separately because dependent claims may add limitations that change the eligibility outcome. The initial burden is on the examiner to explain why a claim is ineligible so the applicant can respond. If the examiner determines it is more likely than not that the claim fails eligibility criteria, formulate an appropriate rejection under Step 1 and/or Step 2B. See MPEP §§2106.03–2106.06 for substantive law, and MPEP §2106.07(a) for drafting rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 Rejection Requirement (Statutory Categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an examiner determines a claim does not fall within a statutory category (Step 1: NO), the rejection must explain why the claim does not fall within one of the four statutory categories of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a reasoned explanation tied to the statutory categories; see MPEP §2106.03 for discussion and guidance on Step 1 analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong One — Identify the Judicial Exception
rubrics_metrics.description: A subject matter eligibility rejection should point to the specific claim limitation(s) that recite the judicial exception and explain why those limitations set forth or describe a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim is directed to an abstract idea, the rejection should identify the abstract idea as recited in the claim and explain why it falls within one of the groupings of abstract ideas (mathematical concepts, mental processes, or certain methods of organizing human activity) enumerated in MPEP §2106.04(a)(2). Where the claim describes but does not expressly set forth the judicial exception, the rejection must explain what subject matter those limitations describe and why the described subject matter is a judicial exception. See MPEP §2106.04 for more information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong Two — Evaluate Integration into a Practical Application
rubrics_metrics.description: For Prong Two, the rejection should identify any additional elements recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception and evaluate whether those elements integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must explain that either 1) there are no additional elements in the claim, or 2) the claim as a whole, looking at additional elements individually and in combination, does not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application using the considerations set forth in MPEP §§2106.04(d), 2106.05(a)-(c) and (e)-(h). Examiners should give weight to all claimed additional elements even if they represent well-understood, routine, conventional activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — Explain Why Additional Elements Do Not Provide 'Significantly More' (Inventive Concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rejection should explain why the additional elements, taken individually and in combination, do not result in the claim, as a whole, amounting to significantly more than the identified judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the examiner concludes certain claim elements recite well-understood, routine, conventional activities, the examiner must expressly support the rejection in writing with one of the four options specified in Subsection III (i.e., provide appropriate factual or evidentiary support). The explanation should cover both individual elements and their combination and be sufficiently clear and specific to enable applicant response. See MPEP §2106.05 et seq. and MPEP §2106.07(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact Prosecution and Complete Examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Regardless of a 35 U.S.C. §101 rejection, examiners must make a complete examination for every claim under the other patentability requirements (35 U.S.C. §§102, 103, 112, and utility, inventorship, and double patenting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under compact prosecution, examiners should state all non-cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action. This ensures the record reflects a complete examination even if a §101 rejection is made.
